newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Scargill to soak the rich, ditch the EU.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Scargill to soak the rich, ditch the EU.

text.p: British miners' leader Arthur Scargill launched the election manifesto of his Socialist Labour Party on Tuesday with a call for the wholesale nationalisation of industry and a complete withdrawal from the European Union.

Scargill, who quit the Labour Party in 1995 after leader Tony Blair ditched its historic commitment to public ownership of industry, said that people earning salaries of more than 80,000 pounds ($130,000) or so should pay 80 percent income tax.
"If someone is in receipt of a million pounds, which is obscene, they should have no difficulty and no objection to accepting a rate of 80 percent," he told a news conference.
Scargill, a hard-left union boss who led an unsuccessful, one-year strike against pit closures in 1983/4, is fielding 65 candidates in the May 1 election.

He has chosen to stand in Wales against Alan Howarth, who defected to Labour in 1995 from the ruling Conservatives, and hopes a commitment to full employment will increase the SLP's vote from the five percent won in recent by-elections.
"Unemployment -- even under this unjust capitalist system -- could be wiped out virtually overnight," the SLP manifesto said.
All it required was a four-day working week, a ban on overtime and retirement on full pay at age 55, he said.

That would cost about 75 billion pounds, Scargill said, but would practically pay for itself since the 50 billion paid on unemployment and related benefits would be saved, while the newly employed would generate more national wealth.

Withdrawal from the European Union -- "the only way that Britain can regain control of its economy and its political powers" -- would save four billion pounds, and 31 billion could easily be found by cutting defence spending by two-thirds.
But ultimately Scargill believes that the money needed to cut the dole queues and revive public services must come from the capitalists.
"There are only two places you can get money -- one is from working men and women, the other is from those who have taken it away from us, and that means big business," Scargill said.
Corporation tax would more than double to generate 50 billion pounds a year rather than the current 23.6 billion.
What if companies decided to relocate overseas if threatened with such tax levels?
"I couldn't care two hoots, bearing in mind that we're going to take their industries into common ownership anyway," Scargill replied.
